questions.concept: Ohm's law is a material statement
questions.question: Why is Ohm's law V = IR not a definition of resistance but a statement about certain materials?
questions.solution: Ohm's law claims R stays CONSTANT as V and I vary — true only for ohmic conductors (metals at constant temperature). Diodes, lamps (heating filament) and electrolytes are non-ohmic: their V–I curve bends. Defining R = V/I is always possible; Ohm's law is the claim that this ratio doesn't change.

questions.question: Resistances combine oppositely to capacitors: series resistances ADD, parallel resistances give less than the smallest. Explain each with current/voltage logic.
questions.solution: Series: the same current must pass through each, voltages add — V = I(R₁+R₂), resistances add. Parallel: all branches share the same V, currents add — I = V(1/R₁ + 1/R₂), so 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ and the total is smaller than either branch (more paths = easier flow). Fixed quantity: current in series, voltage in parallel.

questions.question: State Kirchhoff's two rules and identify the conservation law each expresses.
questions.solution: Junction rule: ΣI_in = ΣI_out at any node — charge cannot accumulate at a point, so charge conservation. Loop rule: ΣΔV = 0 around any closed loop — a charge returning to its start has zero net energy change, so energy conservation. The rules are bookkeeping for the two conserved quantities.

questions.question: A battery reads 12.0 V open-circuit but 11.5 V while driving a load. Explain the difference and define terminal voltage.
questions.solution: The 12.0 V is the emf (no current, no internal drop). Driving current I, the battery's own resistance r drops Ir internally: terminal voltage V = ε − Ir = 11.5 V. The 'missing' 0.5 V heats the battery itself. Measuring both lets you extract r = (ε − V)/I.

questions.question: Why does a load extract maximum power when its resistance equals the battery's internal resistance, even though that wastes half the energy?
questions.solution: P_load = ε²R/(R+r)²: increasing R from 0 raises P (more voltage across the load) until R = r, beyond which the falling current dominates and P declines. At R = r, half the power heats the battery — efficiency is only 50%. Maximum POWER transfer and maximum EFFICIENCY are different goals; matching is for power, high R is for efficiency.
